doc.title: Phil Wilson interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, September 27, 2023

title: The Metropole stage and the 1962 Woody Herman band
summary: He describes the long narrow bandstand over the bar at the Metropole, the mirror used to watch the hi-hat, and Jake Hanna's jokes.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: It wasn’t. Haven’t you ever seen that video? You ought to check it out because I mean Chase and the five trumpets, three trombones you know, four saxophones up there and they — somebody had the smart idea, wouldn’t it be fun to match the early days of Woody Herman’s ’62 band when we played The Metropole in New York, the corner of Seventh and Broadway I think it was, something like that. 48th Street. It was the corner of 48th and Broadway. And every night, this is what put us on the map because they had a picture made up of us and put it on the top of a Billboard issue, on the front page, because it was unheard of. The bar was 75 feet long. People had an open door, open, wide open, I mean really wide — you could park the car in the door. And people coming by the place could just walk in and walk out. I mean it was always open, right at the corner of Broadway and 48th so you know, it was always packed. And the bar went 48 — 75 feet up here is the band — the saxophones close to the door, then they run into Nat Pierce’s piano and this is right behind the bar. And right at this point four saxophones and then you’ve got to have a piano and you couldn’t put — it didn’t fit on the just half the bar so it had to cover the full bar, so all the bartenders if they wanted to go from one end to the other they had to bow their head way, way down. It was unbelievable. But that was the stage. Also that was where Woody could do his act and Charlie “The Arm” — it was four saxophones, Charlie “The Arm,” and then this thing over the bar right, with the drums and the piano and Woody. And then five trumpets over here and the three trombones way down there. Holy shit! And I was — you know I was a regular feature, I was blessed with that. And every time I had to play a solo I had to walk up in front of five trumpets to get to the microphone.
It was a very narrow stage, wasn’t it?

Yes. Because the gentleman who started this whole project, the Hamilton graduate, talked about going there. The band would be in a straight line and boy, you have to listen really hard and listen in a different fashion.

Yeah. And you better know it. It was a different fashion. And the opposite side of the room, it was a long room, not terribly wide okay? So the far — opposite the stage over there was a wall, ceiling to floor mirror. So that we could watch Jake Hanna’s hi-hat. You know what I mean? © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

And that would keep it together. And that’s exactly what we did. And during the third set, and the third set would usually go on around 2:30 in the morning. We started at 10. And when we’d get around to the third set every once in a while Jake, who had a sharp sense of humor, would start playing on one and three instead of two and four. And it made some interesting blips.
Yeah. Instead of sight reading you were sight playing.
